subject: psad
title: Principles of Structural Analysis and Design

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Reaction of a simple beam under an off-center point load
questions.stem: A simply supported beam AB has a span of 6 m. A concentrated load of 30 kN acts 2 m from support A. Neglecting the beam's weight, what is the reaction at A?
given: Span $L = 6\text{ m}$ (simple supports at A and B)
Point load $P = 30\text{ kN}$ at $a = 2\text{ m}$ from A
questions.required: The vertical reaction $R_A$ at support A.

formulas.label: Moment equilibrium about B
formulas.tex: \sum M_B = 0:\quad R_A L - P b = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; R_A = \frac{Pb}{L}

variables.meaning: Distance from the load to support B

solution.title: Locate the load relative to B
solution.text: The load is 2 m from A, so it is $b = 6 - 2 = 4$ m from B.

questions.insight: Each reaction is proportional to the distance to the **far** support, so the support nearer the load carries the larger share.
commonErrors: Using the distance to the near support ($Pa/L = 10$ kN), which gives $R_B$ instead of $R_A$.
Splitting the load equally (15 kN) as if it were at midspan.

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Normal stress in a solid circular rod
questions.stem: A solid steel rod with a diameter of 20 mm carries an axial tensile load of 50 kN. What is the normal stress in the rod?
questions.required: The normal stress $\sigma$ in the rod.

solution.title: Compute the area
solution.text: Use the diameter in the circle-area formula.

solution.title: Compute the stress
solution.text: Divide the load in newtons by the area in mm² to get MPa.

questions.insight: Keeping loads in N and areas in mm² gives stresses directly in MPa; the result is well below the yield strength of ordinary structural steel.
commonErrors: Using the diameter as the radius ($A = \pi(20)^2$), giving 39.79 MPa.
Using a square area $d^2 = 400$ mm², giving 125 MPa.
Using the radius in $\pi d^2/4$ (i.e. $A = \pi(10)^2/4$), giving 636.62 MPa.

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Thermal stress in a bar with an initial gap
questions.stem: A steel bar 5 m long is placed between two rigid walls with a gap of 1.0 mm at one end at the initial temperature. The temperature then rises by 50 °C. Use $\alpha = 11.7\times10^{-6}$ /°C and $E = 200$ GPa. What is the resulting compressive stress in the bar?
questions.required: The compressive stress $\sigma$ in the bar after the temperature rise.

solution.title: Free expansion
solution.text: Compute the elongation if the bar were unrestrained.

solution.title: Check the gap
solution.text: Since $2.925 > 1.0$ mm, the gap closes and the walls prevent the remaining expansion.

solution.title: Stress from the restrained elongation
solution.text: The wall force must shorten the bar by 1.925 mm. From $\delta = \sigma L/E$:

questions.insight: A small gap relieves a large share of thermal stress: here it removes about one third of the 117 MPa that would develop with no gap.
commonErrors: Ignoring the gap and using $E\alpha\Delta T = 117.0$ MPa.
Adding the gap to the thermal expansion instead of subtracting it (157.0 MPa).
Computing the stress from the gap alone, $E e/L = 40.0$ MPa.

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Reaction of an overhanging beam
questions.stem: Beam ABC is 8 m long, with a pin support at A ($x = 0$) and a roller at B ($x = 6$ m), so BC is a 2-m overhang. The beam carries a uniform load of 10 kN/m over its entire 8-m length and a concentrated load of 20 kN at the free end C. What is the vertical reaction at A?
given: Pin at A ($x = 0$), roller at B ($x = 6$ m), free end C ($x = 8$ m)
Uniform load $w = 10\text{ kN/m}$ over the full 8 m

solution.title: Resultant of the uniform load
solution.text: The 80-kN resultant acts at $x = 4$ m; the total load is $80 + 20 = 100$ kN.

solution.title: Moments about B
solution.text: Loads beyond B act on the opposite side of B.

questions.insight: Loads on an overhang lift the far support: the 20-kN end load alone reduces $R_A$ by about 6.7 kN.
commonErrors: Reporting $R_B = 80$ kN as the reaction at A.
Including only the 60 kN of uniform load between the supports while still using the full total load for vertical equilibrium (43.3 kN).
Treating the beam as a simple span with symmetrical reactions and ignoring the overhang (30 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum moment of a uniformly loaded simple beam
questions.stem: A simply supported beam with a span of 8 m carries a uniform load of 12 kN/m (including its own weight) over the entire span. What is the maximum bending moment?

solution.title: Reactions
solution.text: Each reaction is $wL/2 = 48$ kN, and the shear is zero at midspan.

solution.title: Maximum moment
solution.text: The maximum moment equals the area of the shear triangle from the support to midspan.

questions.insight: The moment at any section equals the area of the shear diagram up to that section, so the peak moment occurs where the shear is zero.
commonErrors: Using the cantilever formula $wL^2/2$ (384 kN·m).
Reporting the reaction or maximum shear, $wL/2 = 48$, as the moment.
Using $wL^2/4$ (192 kN·m), confusing the uniform-load case with the point-load coefficient.
relatedConcepts: Relationship between load, shear and moment

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum moment under combined uniform and point loads
questions.stem: A simply supported beam with a span of 6 m carries a uniform load of 10 kN/m over the entire span and a concentrated load of 40 kN located 2 m from the left support A. What is the maximum bending moment in the beam?
given: Point load $P = 40\text{ kN}$ at 2 m from A

solution.title: Locate zero shear
solution.text: Just left of the load $V = 56.67 - 10(2) = 36.67$ kN; just right of it $V = 36.67 - 40 = -3.33$ kN. The shear changes sign at $x = 2$ m.

questions.insight: Maxima from separate load cases cannot simply be added unless they occur at the same section; always locate the point of zero shear for the combined loading.
commonErrors: Adding $wL^2/8 = 45$ and $Pab/L = 53.33$ (98.33 kN·m); these maxima occur at different sections.
Adding $wL^2/8$ and $PL/4$ (105 kN·m), treating the point load as if it were at midspan.
Forgetting the moment of the uniform load to the left of the section (113.33 kN·m).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Tip deflection of a cantilever with an end load
questions.stem: A steel cantilever beam 3 m long carries a concentrated load of 20 kN at its free end. $E = 200$ GPa and $I = 60\times10^6$ mm⁴. Neglecting the beam's weight, what is the deflection at the free end?
questions.required: The deflection $\delta$ at the free end.
questions.insight: Deflection grows with the cube of the length, so doubling the cantilever length multiplies the tip deflection by eight.
commonErrors: Using the uniform-load cantilever coefficient $1/8$ (5.63 mm).
Omitting the factor 3 in the denominator (45.00 mm).
Using the simple-beam midspan coefficient $1/48$ (0.94 mm).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Tie force in a triangular roof truss
questions.stem: A symmetrical triangular roof truss has a span of 8 m and a rise of 3 m. Its two rafters meet at the apex, and a horizontal tie connects the two supports (pin at one end, roller at the other). A single vertical load of 60 kN acts at the apex. What is the force in the horizontal tie?
given: Span 8 m, rise 3 m (each rafter: 4 m horizontal, 3 m vertical)
questions.required: The force $F_T$ in the horizontal tie.

solution.title: Reactions and geometry
solution.text: By symmetry each reaction is $60/2 = 30$ kN. Each rafter spans 4 m horizontally and 3 m vertically, so its length is 5 m.

solution.title: Rafter force
solution.text: Vertical equilibrium of the support joint gives the rafter force (compression).

solution.title: Tie force
solution.text: Horizontal equilibrium of the same joint gives the tie force (tension).

questions.insight: A flatter roof (smaller rise) increases both rafter and tie forces for the same apex load.
commonErrors: Reporting the rafter force (50 kN compression) instead of the tie force.
Swapping the sine and cosine of the rafter slope, giving $30(3/4) = 22.5$ kN.
Reporting the support reaction (30 kN) as the tie force.

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Slenderness ratio of a solid circular strut
questions.stem: A solid circular steel strut has a diameter of 40 mm and a length of 2 m. Both ends are pinned. What is its slenderness ratio $KL/r$?
questions.insight: The radius of gyration of a solid circle is only a quarter of its diameter, so slender round bars reach high slenderness ratios quickly.
commonErrors: Using the geometric radius $d/2 = 20$ mm as the radius of gyration (100).
Using the diameter in place of $r$ (50).
Using $K = 2.0$ (fixed–free) instead of 1.0 (400).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Nominal moment strength of a singly reinforced beam
questions.stem: A rectangular concrete beam is 300 mm wide with a total depth of 560 mm and an effective depth of 500 mm. It is reinforced with three 25-mm diameter tension bars. Use $f'_c = 28$ MPa and $f_y = 420$ MPa, and assume the steel yields. What is the nominal moment strength $M_n$?

solution.title: Verify yielding
solution.text: With $\beta_1 = 0.85$: $c = 86.62/0.85 = 101.9$ mm and the steel strain far exceeds $f_y/E_s = 0.0021$.

solution.title: Nominal moment
solution.text: Use the effective depth as the reference.

questions.insight: The internal lever arm $d - a/2$ is about 91% of $d$ here, typical of lightly reinforced, ductile beams.
commonErrors: Reporting the design strength $\phi M_n = 0.90(282.5) = 254.2$ kN·m when $M_n$ was asked.
Using the total depth $h = 560$ mm instead of $d$ (319.6 kN·m).
Ignoring the stress-block depth and using a lever arm of $d$ (309.3 kN·m).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Required tension steel for a factored moment
questions.stem: A singly reinforced rectangular beam with $b = 300$ mm and $d = 500$ mm must resist a factored moment $M_u = 250$ kN·m. Use $f'_c = 28$ MPa, $f_y = 420$ MPa, $\beta_1 = 0.85$ and $\phi = 0.90$ (verify that the section is tension-controlled, $\varepsilon_t \ge 0.005$). What is the required area of tension steel?

variables.meaning: Net tensile strain in the steel

solution.title: Express a in terms of A_s
Solve the quadratic
solution.text: Rearrange and take the smaller root.

questions.insight: Because $\varepsilon_t$ is well above 0.005, the assumed $\phi = 0.90$ is valid and no iteration is needed.
commonErrors: Designing for $M_u$ without dividing by $\phi$ (1288 mm²).
Multiplying by $\phi$ instead of dividing, i.e. using $0.90M_u$ as the nominal moment (1026 mm²).
Assuming a lever arm of $0.85d$ instead of solving for $a$ (1556 mm²).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Euler load of a column with unequal moments of inertia
questions.stem: A 5-m steel column is pinned at both ends and is unbraced about both axes. Its section has $I_x = 80\times10^6$ mm⁴ and $I_y = 25\times10^6$ mm⁴. With $E = 200$ GPa, what is the Euler critical load? Assume elastic buckling governs.

solution.title: Governing axis
solution.text: Both axes have the same effective length ($KL = 5000$ mm), so the smaller moment of inertia governs.

solution.title: Euler load
solution.text: Apply Euler's formula in N and mm.

questions.insight: A column buckles about the axis with the largest effective slenderness; bracing the weak axis at midheight would quadruple its weak-axis Euler load.
commonErrors: Using the strong-axis $I_x$ (6316.5 kN).
Using $K = 2.0$ (fixed–free) instead of 1.0 (493.5 kN).
Using $K = 0.5$ (fixed–fixed) instead of 1.0 (7895.7 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Force to start a crate up an incline
questions.stem: A 500-N crate rests on a plank inclined at $25^\circ$ to the horizontal in a construction-site loading ramp. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the plank is 0.30. What force $P$, applied parallel to the incline, is required to start moving the crate **up** the incline?
questions.required: The force $P$ for impending motion up the incline.

variables.meaning: Applied force parallel to the incline

solution.title: Normal force
solution.text: Resolve the weight perpendicular to the incline.

solution.title: Friction at impending motion
solution.text: Friction acts **down** the incline, opposing the impending upward motion.

solution.title: Equilibrium along the incline
solution.text: The weight component along the incline is $500\sin 25^\circ = 211.31$ N.

questions.insight: Friction adds to the gravity component when pushing up the slope, but subtracts when merely holding the crate from sliding down; the two cases differ by $2\mu_s N$.
commonErrors: Letting friction act up the incline (as if preventing sliding down), giving 75.4 N.
Ignoring friction entirely, giving 211.3 N.
Multiplying $\mu_s$ by the full weight instead of the normal force, giving 361.3 N.
relatedConcepts: Impending motion on an inclined plane

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Centroidal moment of inertia of a T-section
questions.stem: A T-section consists of a flange 200 mm wide by 20 mm thick on top of a web 20 mm thick by 180 mm deep (overall depth 200 mm). Determine the moment of inertia of the section about its horizontal centroidal axis.
questions.required: The moment of inertia $\bar{I}_x$ about the horizontal centroidal axis.

variables.meaning: Centroid height measured from the bottom of the web
Distance from each part's centroid to the section centroid

solution.title: Areas and centroids
solution.text: Measure $y$ from the bottom of the web. Flange: $A_1 = 4000$ mm² at $y_1 = 190$ mm. Web: $A_2 = 3600$ mm² at $y_2 = 90$ mm.

solution.title: Own moments of inertia
solution.text: Each rectangle about its own centroid:

questions.insight: The transfer ($Ad^2$) terms supply about two-thirds of the total here, which is why material placed far from the neutral axis is so effective in bending.
commonErrors: Adding only the rectangles' own centroidal values and omitting the $Ad^2$ terms (9.85 × 10⁶ mm⁴).
Taking the axis at mid-depth (100 mm) instead of at the true centroid (42.61 × 10⁶ mm⁴).
Computing the moment of inertia about the bottom of the web (183.4 × 10⁶ mm⁴).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Skidding distance on a downgrade
questions.stem: A 1,200-kg service vehicle travelling at 80 km/h on a road with a **4% downgrade** locks its wheels and skids to a stop. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the tires and the pavement is 0.55. Use $g = 9.81$ m/s². What is the skidding distance?
questions.required: The skidding distance $s$ until the vehicle stops.

solution.title: Deceleration
solution.text: Newton's second law along the road: friction $\mu_k mg\cos\theta$ acts uphill while the gravity component $mg\sin\theta$ acts downhill. The mass cancels.

questions.insight: Even a mild 4% downgrade lengthens the stopping distance by about 8% compared with level road, which is why stopping-sight-distance tables include a grade correction.
commonErrors: Ignoring the grade and using $a = \mu_k g$ (45.76 m).
Treating the grade as uphill so gravity helps stop the vehicle (42.69 m).
Omitting the factor 2 in $s = v_0^2/(2a)$ (98.78 m).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Tension in two cables supporting a load
questions.stem: A 12-kN precast panel hangs from ring C, which is held by two cables. Cable AC goes up to the left at $25^\circ$ above the horizontal and cable BC goes up to the right at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal. What is the tension in cable BC?
given: Cable AC at $25^\circ$ above the horizontal (to the left)
Cable BC at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal (to the right)

formulas.label: Equilibrium of a concurrent force system

solution.title: Vertical equilibrium
solution.text: The vertical components carry the load.

solution.title: Solve
solution.text: Substituting $T_{AC} = T_{BC}\cos 60^\circ/\cos 25^\circ$ and simplifying gives $T_{BC} = W\cos 25^\circ/\sin(25^\circ + 60^\circ)$.

questions.insight: The steeper cable carries the larger share of the load; as the two cables approach horizontal, both tensions grow without bound.
commonErrors: Reporting $T_{AC}$ (6.02 kN) instead of $T_{BC}$.
Using the sine of the other cable's angle instead of its cosine in the horizontal balance (5.09 kN).
Dividing the load by the sum of the sines, as if both tensions were equal (9.31 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Stress in the bars of a short composite column
questions.stem: A short reinforced concrete pedestal is 300 mm × 300 mm and contains four 25-mm diameter steel bars. It carries an axial service load of 1,200 kN. Assume both materials remain elastic and are perfectly bonded, with $E_s = 200$ GPa and $E_c = 25$ GPa. What is the stress in the steel bars?
questions.required: The axial stress $f_s$ in the steel bars.

formulas.label: Equilibrium
formulas.tex: P = f_c A_c + f_s A_s = f_c(A_c + nA_s)

solution.title: Areas
solution.text: Steel area and net concrete area:

solution.title: Modular ratio
solution.text: Equal strains mean the steel stress is $n$ times the concrete stress.

questions.insight: Although the bars occupy only about 2% of the section, they carry roughly 15% of the load because steel is eight times stiffer than concrete.
commonErrors: Using the gross area for an average stress and multiplying by $n$ (106.67 MPa).
Reporting the concrete stress (11.57 MPa) instead of the steel stress.
Treating the section as homogeneous, $P/A_g$ (13.33 MPa).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Shear stress in a shaft transmitting power
questions.stem: A solid steel shaft 70 mm in diameter transmits 150 kW at 300 rpm in a pumping station. What is the maximum torsional shear stress in the shaft?

solution.title: Frequency
solution.text: Convert rpm to revolutions per second.

solution.title: Maximum shear stress
solution.text: Use N and mm to obtain MPa.

questions.insight: For a given power, torque is inversely proportional to speed, so slow-turning shafts must be thicker.
commonErrors: Using $32T/(\pi d^3)$, the coefficient for bending stress (141.8 MPa).
Dividing power by rpm directly, $T = P/N$, without converting to rad/s (7.42 MPa).
Using the radius (35 mm) in place of the diameter (567.2 MPa).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Angle of twist of a hollow shaft
questions.stem: A hollow steel shaft 2 m long has an outside diameter of 100 mm and an inside diameter of 80 mm. It is subjected to a torque of 8 kN·m. Using $G = 80$ GPa, what is the angle of twist between its ends, in degrees?
questions.required: The angle of twist $\theta$ in degrees.

solution.title: Angle of twist in radians
solution.text: Use consistent N and mm units.

questions.insight: Removing the inner 80 mm takes away 64% of the material but only 41% of the torsional stiffness, which is why hollow shafts are efficient.
commonErrors: Ignoring the hole and using the solid-shaft $J$ (1.167°).
Using $\pi/64$ (the moment of inertia $I$) instead of $\pi/32$ for $J$ (3.954°).
Using the elastic modulus $E = 200$ GPa instead of the shear modulus $G$ (0.791°).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum bending stress in a rectangular beam
questions.stem: A simply supported rectangular beam 150 mm wide and 300 mm deep spans 4 m and carries a uniform load of 15 kN/m (including its own weight). The beam is placed with its 300-mm dimension vertical. What is the maximum flexural stress?

solution.title: Maximum moment
solution.text: For a simple span with uniform load:

solution.title: Stress
solution.text: Divide the moment in N·mm by $S$.

questions.insight: Bending stress varies with the square of the depth, so the same beam laid flat would be stressed twice as much.
commonErrors: Interchanging $b$ and $h$ (beam laid flat), giving 26.67 MPa.
Forgetting the 6 in $S = bh^2/6$, giving 2.22 MPa.
Using the moment of inertia about the base, $bh^3/3$, with $c = h/2$ (3.33 MPa).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum shear stress in a built-up I-section
questions.stem: A welded steel I-section has two flanges, each 200 mm × 20 mm, and a web 10 mm thick and 260 mm deep (overall depth 300 mm). At a certain section the vertical shear is 150 kN. Using $\tau = VQ/(Ib)$, what is the maximum shear stress in the web?
questions.required: The maximum shear stress $\tau_{\max}$ (at the neutral axis).

formulas.label: Moment of inertia of a symmetric I

variables.meaning: First moment of the area above the neutral axis
Width at the level considered (web thickness)

solution.title: Moment of inertia
solution.text: Outer rectangle minus the two side voids.

solution.title: First moment above the neutral axis
solution.text: Flange: $4000$ mm² at 140 mm; upper half of web: $10 \times 130$ at 65 mm.

solution.title: Shear stress at the neutral axis
solution.text: The width at the neutral axis is the web thickness, 10 mm.

questions.insight: In I-sections the web carries nearly all the shear, so the quick estimate $V/(d\,t_w)$ is a fair approximation, though here it underestimates the peak by about 11%.
commonErrors: Including only the flange in $Q$ (48.92 MPa), which gives the stress at the web–flange junction rather than the maximum.
Using the average web shear $V/(d\,t_w)$ (50.00 MPa).
Dividing by the flange width (200 mm) instead of the web thickness (2.82 MPa).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Minimum wall thickness of a pressurized cylindrical tank
questions.stem: A cylindrical steel water-pressure tank has an inside diameter of 2.0 m and must hold an internal pressure of 1.8 MPa. If the allowable tensile stress in the plate is 140 MPa, what is the minimum wall thickness required? Treat the tank as thin-walled and ignore joint efficiency.

solution.title: Governing stress
solution.text: The hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, so it governs.

solution.title: Thickness
solution.text: Set the hoop stress equal to the allowable stress.

questions.insight: Cylindrical shells are twice as stressed circumferentially as longitudinally, which is why seams running along the length are the critical joints.
commonErrors: Designing for the longitudinal stress $pD/(4t)$ (6.43 mm).
Omitting the 2 in the hoop-stress formula (25.71 mm).
Substituting the radius for the diameter in the longitudinal-stress formula (3.21 mm).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum principal stress from plane stress
questions.stem: At a point on the web of a loaded girder, the state of plane stress is $\sigma_x = 80$ MPa (tension), $\sigma_y = 40$ MPa (compression) and $\tau_{xy} = 30$ MPa. What is the maximum principal stress?

solution.title: Center of Mohr's circle
solution.text: Average normal stress, with tension positive:

solution.title: Radius
solution.text: The radius equals the maximum in-plane shear stress.

solution.title: Maximum principal stress
solution.text: Add the radius to the center.

questions.insight: The shear stress raises the peak normal stress about 9% above $\sigma_x$; the minimum principal stress is $\sigma_2 = -47.08$ MPa.
commonErrors: Reporting the radius (maximum in-plane shear, 67.08 MPa) instead of $\sigma_1$.
Ignoring the shear stress and taking $\sigma_x = 80$ MPa as the maximum.
Forgetting to halve $(\sigma_x - \sigma_y)$ under the square root (143.69 MPa).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Rigid bar supported by steel and aluminum rods
questions.stem: A rigid horizontal bar ABC, 3 m long, is hinged at A ($x = 0$). It is held horizontal by two vertical hangers: an aluminum rod at B ($x = 1.5$ m; length 1.5 m, $A = 500$ mm², $E = 70$ GPa) and a steel rod at C ($x = 3.0$ m; length 2.0 m, $A = 300$ mm², $E = 200$ GPa). Both rods are initially stress-free. A load of 50 kN is then applied to the bar at $x = 2.5$ m. Neglecting the bar's weight, what is the stress in the steel rod?
given: Hinge at A; rods at $x = 1.5$ m (aluminum) and $x = 3.0$ m (steel)
questions.required: The normal stress $\sigma_s$ in the steel rod.

solution.title: Rod flexibilities
solution.text: $L/(AE)$ for each rod, in mm per N:

solution.title: Compatibility
solution.text: The rigid bar rotates about A, so $\delta_s = 2\delta_a$.

solution.title: Equilibrium
solution.text: Substitute into the moment equation about A.

solution.title: Steel force and stress
solution.text: Back-substitute and divide by the steel area.

questions.insight: The farther, stiffer support attracts more load: the steel rod carries about 72% of the total hanger force even though it is longer.
commonErrors: Assuming both rods stretch equally ($\delta_s = \delta_a$) instead of in proportion to their distances from the hinge (100.00 MPa).
Ignoring the aluminum rod and taking moments about A with only the steel rod (138.89 MPa).
Reporting the aluminum stress (27.13 MPa) instead of the steel stress.

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum moment under a triangular load
questions.stem: A simply supported beam AB spans 6 m. It carries a distributed load that increases linearly from zero at A to 30 kN/m at B (for example, soil or water pressure on a vertical member). What is the maximum bending moment in the beam?
given: Triangular load: 0 at A to $w_0 = 30\text{ kN/m}$ at B
questions.required: The maximum bending moment $M_{\max}$ and its location.

solution.title: Reactions
solution.text: Total load $= \tfrac{1}{2}(30)(6) = 90$ kN acting $2L/3 = 4$ m from A.

questions.insight: The peak moment shifts toward the heavier end of the load ($x = 0.577L$); its value $w_0L^2/(9\sqrt{3})$ is only slightly above the midspan moment.
commonErrors: Assuming the maximum occurs at midspan (67.50 kN·m).
Using the uniform-load formula $w_0L^2/8$ with the peak intensity (135.0 kN·m).
Using the fixed-end coefficient $w_0L^2/12$ (90.0 kN·m).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Midspan deflection by superposition
questions.stem: A simply supported steel beam spans 7.5 m. It carries a uniform load of 18 kN/m over the full span plus a concentrated load of 60 kN at midspan. $E = 200$ GPa and $I = 350\times10^6$ mm⁴. What is the total midspan deflection?

solution.title: Superpose
solution.text: Both maxima occur at midspan, so they add directly.

questions.insight: Superposition is valid because the beam is linear-elastic, and here both component maxima fall at the same point; the total is about $L/414$.
commonErrors: Including only the uniform load (10.59 mm).
Dropping the factor 5 in the uniform-load formula (9.65 mm).
Lumping the whole uniform load with $P$ into one midspan point load, $(wL + P)L^3/(48EI)$ (24.48 mm).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Free-end deflection of a cantilever with two loads
questions.stem: A 4-m steel cantilever carries a uniform load of 12 kN/m over its whole length and a concentrated load of 15 kN located 2.5 m from the fixed support. $E = 200$ GPa and $I = 120\times10^6$ mm⁴. What is the deflection at the free end?
given: $P = 15\text{ kN}$ at $a = 2.5\text{ m}$ from the fixed end

formulas.label: Point load at a from the support (tip deflection)

variables.meaning: Distance of the point load from the fixed end

solution.title: Uniform load
solution.text: Tip deflection from the full-length uniform load:

solution.title: Point load
solution.text: Under the load the deflection is $Pa^3/(3EI) = 3.255$ mm and the slope is $Pa^2/(2EI)$; beyond the load the beam stays straight, giving the combined formula:

questions.insight: The unloaded segment beyond a point load does not bend, but it rotates with the slope at the load, so its tip deflection is more than the deflection under the load.
commonErrors: Treating the 15-kN load as if it acted at the tip, $PL^3/(3EI)$ (29.33 mm).
Using only the deflection under the point load, $Pa^3/(3EI)$, and forgetting the rotation of the free segment (19.26 mm).
Ignoring the point load entirely (16.00 mm).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Top-chord force in a Pratt truss by the method of sections
questions.stem: A parallel-chord Pratt truss has six equal panels of 3 m (span 18 m) and a depth of 4 m. The bottom-chord joints are L0 to L6, and the top-chord joints U1 to U5 lie directly above L1 to L5. In the third panel the diagonal runs from U2 down to L3. The truss is supported by a pin at L0 and a roller at L6 and carries a vertical load of 20 kN at each of the bottom joints L1 to L5. What is the force in top-chord member U2–U3?
given: Six panels at 3 m; depth $h = 4\text{ m}$
Loads: 20 kN at each of L1, L2, L3, L4, L5
Pin at L0, roller at L6; diagonal of panel 3 from U2 to L3
questions.required: The force in member U2–U3 and whether it is tension or compression.

formulas.label: Method of sections
formulas.tex: \sum M_{L3} = 0 \text{ on the left free body}

solution.title: Reactions
solution.text: The loading is symmetric: total load 100 kN.

solution.title: Cut the truss
solution.text: Pass a section through panel 3, cutting U2–U3, U2–L3 and L2–L3. Diagonal U2–L3 and chord L2–L3 both pass through L3, so take moments about L3 ($x = 9$ m) for the left part.

solution.title: Moments about L3
solution.text: Assume the top-chord force pulls away from U2 (tension) at a lever arm of 4 m.

solution.title: Interpret
solution.text: The negative sign means the assumed tension is wrong.

questions.insight: Chord forces follow the bending-moment diagram of an equivalent beam divided by the truss depth, so they peak near midspan.
commonErrors: Taking moments about L2 instead of L3, which gives the bottom-chord force of panel 3 (60.0 kN tension).
Forgetting the panel loads to the left of the section (112.5 kN).
Omitting the load at L1 (82.5 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum positive moment in a propped cantilever
questions.stem: A beam 6 m long is fixed at end A and simply supported (propped) at end B. It carries a uniform load of 24 kN/m over its entire length. EI is constant. What is the maximum **positive** bending moment in the span?
given: Span $L = 6\text{ m}$, fixed at A, propped at B

formulas.label: Prop reaction (compatibility: zero deflection at B)

solution.title: Prop reaction
solution.text: Remove the prop, then restore zero deflection at B.

questions.insight: The fixed-end moment ($wL^2/8 = 108$ kN·m, hogging) is the largest moment in the beam; the positive span moment is only about 56% of it.
commonErrors: Reporting $wL^2/8$ (108.0 kN·m), which is the negative moment at the fixed end (or the simple-beam moment).
Evaluating the moment at midspan instead of at the point of zero shear (54.0 kN·m).
Using the fixed–fixed end moment $wL^2/12$ (72.0 kN·m).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Middle reaction of a two-span continuous beam
questions.stem: A continuous beam ABC is simply supported at A, B and C, with span AB = 6 m and span BC = 4 m. Both spans carry a uniform load of 20 kN/m, and EI is constant. Using the three-moment equation, what is the vertical reaction at the interior support B?
given: Simple supports at A, B, C ($M_A = M_C = 0$); constant EI

solution.title: Shear just left of B
solution.text: Free body AB: the hogging moment at B increases the shear at B.

solution.title: Shear just right of B and reaction

questions.insight: Continuity transfers load toward the interior support: $R_B$ is about 29% larger than the 100 kN given by treating each span as simply supported.
commonErrors: Treating the spans as two simple beams and ignoring continuity (100.0 kN).
Using the equal-span coefficient $1.25wL$ with the average span of 5 m (125.0 kN).
Subtracting the $M_B/L$ terms instead of adding them (70.83 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Neutral-axis depth of a singly reinforced beam
questions.stem: A rectangular beam 250 mm wide is reinforced with tension steel of area 1,500 mm². The concrete strength is $f'_c = 35$ MPa, the steel yields at $f_y = 415$ MPa, and $\beta_1 = 0.80$ for this concrete. Using the Whitney rectangular stress block (strength design, ACI 318 / NSCP 2015 approach), what is the depth $c$ from the extreme compression fiber to the neutral axis?

variables.meaning: Depth of the equivalent stress block

questions.insight: For stronger concrete $\beta_1$ drops below 0.85, so the neutral axis lies proportionally deeper than the stress block.
commonErrors: Reporting the stress-block depth $a$ (83.70 mm) as $c$.
Using $\beta_1 = 0.85$ instead of the stated 0.80 (98.47 mm).
Omitting the 0.85 factor on $f'_c$ (88.93 mm).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum steel for a tension-controlled section
questions.stem: A singly reinforced rectangular beam has $b = 300$ mm and $d = 520$ mm, with $f'_c = 28$ MPa and $f_y = 420$ MPa. Use $\varepsilon_{cu} = 0.003$ and $\beta_1 = 0.85$. What is the largest tension steel area for which the section is still tension-controlled, i.e. the net tensile strain is exactly $\varepsilon_t = 0.005$?
questions.insight: This limit is about 64% of the balanced steel area; staying below it lets the designer use the full $\phi = 0.90$.
commonErrors: Computing the balanced steel area with $c_b = 600d/(600 + f_y)$ (4420.0 mm²).
Using the older minimum-strain limit $\varepsilon_t = 0.004$ (3220.3 mm²).
Forgetting $\beta_1$ and taking $a = c$ (3315.0 mm²).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Design moment of a beam in the transition zone
questions.stem: A rectangular beam has $b = 300$ mm and $d = 450$ mm and is reinforced with four 28-mm tension bars. Use $f'_c = 21$ MPa, $f_y = 415$ MPa, $E_s = 200$ GPa, $\varepsilon_{cu} = 0.003$ and $\beta_1 = 0.85$. Take $\phi = 0.90$ if $\varepsilon_t \ge 0.005$, $\phi = 0.65$ if $\varepsilon_t \le \varepsilon_y$, and $\phi = 0.65 + 0.25(\varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_y)/(0.005 - \varepsilon_y)$ in between. Assuming the steel yields (verify), what is the design moment strength $\phi M_n$?

solution.title: Strength reduction factor
solution.text: Since $0.002075 < \varepsilon_t < 0.005$, the steel yields but the section is in the transition zone.

questions.insight: Heavily reinforced beams lose capacity through the reduced $\phi$: adding steel past the tension-controlled limit raises $M_n$ but buys much less $\phi M_n$.
commonErrors: Using $\phi = 0.90$ without checking $\varepsilon_t$ (326.2 kN·m).
Treating the section as compression-controlled, $\phi = 0.65$ (235.6 kN·m).
Reporting $M_n$ (362.4 kN·m) instead of $\phi M_n$.

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Nominal shear strength of concrete in a beam
questions.stem: A normal-weight concrete beam ($\lambda = 1.0$) has a web width of 300 mm and an effective depth of 500 mm, with $f'_c = 28$ MPa. Using the simplified expression $V_c = 0.17\lambda\sqrt{f'_c}\,b_wd$ (with $f'_c$ in MPa), what is the nominal shear strength provided by the concrete?

solution.title: Square root of f'c
solution.text: Only the square root of $f'_c$ enters the formula.

questions.insight: The design value is $\phi V_c = 0.75V_c$; stirrups become mandatory (in most beams) once $V_u$ exceeds half of that.
commonErrors: Reporting the design value $\phi V_c$ with $\phi = 0.75$ (101.20 kN) when $V_c$ was asked.
Using the two-way (punching) coefficient 0.33 (261.93 kN).
Reporting the minimum-stirrup threshold $\phi V_c/2$ (50.60 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Required stirrup spacing for a factored shear
questions.stem: At the critical section of a rectangular beam ($b_w = 300$ mm, $d = 450$ mm), the factored shear is $V_u = 220$ kN. Use $f'_c = 21$ MPa (normal weight), $V_c = 0.17\sqrt{f'_c}\,b_wd$, $\phi = 0.75$ and vertical two-legged 10-mm stirrups with $f_{yt} = 275$ MPa. What stirrup spacing is required for strength (before rounding down to a practical value or applying maximum-spacing limits)?
questions.insight: Because $V_s = 188.16$ kN is below $0.33\sqrt{f'_c}\,b_wd = 204.2$ kN, the maximum spacing is $d/2 = 225$ mm, so strength governs; a practical choice is 100 mm.
commonErrors: Forgetting to divide $V_u$ by $\phi$ (169.3 mm).
Using the area of one leg only (51.7 mm).
Ignoring the concrete contribution $V_c$ (66.3 mm).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum design axial strength of a tied column
questions.stem: A short tied column is 400 mm × 400 mm and is reinforced with eight 25-mm longitudinal bars. Use $f'_c = 28$ MPa and $f_y = 420$ MPa. For a tied column take $\phi = 0.65$ and limit the axial strength to $0.80P_o$, where $P_o = 0.85f'_c(A_g - A_{st}) + f_yA_{st}$. What is the maximum design axial strength $\phi P_{n,\max}$?
questions.required: The maximum design axial strength $\phi P_{n,\max}$.

solution.title: Nominal concentric capacity
solution.text: Concrete on the net area plus steel.

questions.insight: The 0.80 cap stands in for the accidental eccentricity every real column has; a spirally reinforced column would use 0.85 and $\phi = 0.75$.
commonErrors: Omitting the 0.80 accidental-eccentricity factor (3486.5 kN).
Using the spiral-column factors $0.85$ and $\phi = 0.75$ (3419.5 kN).
Applying 0.80 but forgetting $\phi$ (4291.1 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Factored one-way shear in a square footing
questions.stem: A 400-mm square column carries a service dead load of 800 kN and a service live load of 500 kN. It rests on a 2.6 m × 2.6 m square footing with an effective depth of 500 mm. Using the load combination $1.2D + 1.6L$ and a uniform factored soil pressure (neglect the footing and soil weight), what is the factored one-way (beam) shear $V_u$ at the critical section located a distance $d$ from the face of the column?
questions.required: The factored one-way shear $V_u$ at $d$ from the column face.

solution.title: Tributary strip
solution.text: Distance from the critical section to the footing edge.

questions.insight: Only the soil pressure outside the critical section loads it; this value is then compared with $\phi V_c$ of the 2.6-m-wide footing section.
commonErrors: Using service loads instead of factored loads (300.0 kN).
Taking the critical section at the face of the column instead of at $d$ from it (744.6 kN).
Measuring $d$ from the footing centerline instead of the column face (541.5 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Bottom-fiber stress from an eccentric prestress
questions.stem: A rectangular pretensioned beam is 300 mm wide and 600 mm deep. At transfer the prestressing force is 1,000 kN, applied 150 mm below the centroid. Considering the prestress only (ignore the beam's self-weight) and taking compression as positive, what is the stress at the bottom fiber?

solution.title: Bending component
solution.text: The eccentric force compresses the bottom fiber.

questions.insight: The same prestress produces $-2.78$ MPa (tension) at the top fiber, which is why transfer checks govern the top fiber of beams with large eccentricities.
commonErrors: Using only the axial component $P/A$ (5.56 MPa).
Using $S = bh^2/12$, which doubles the bending term (22.22 MPa).
Using only the bending component $Pe/S$ (8.33 MPa).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Bottom-fiber stress of a prestressed beam at service
questions.stem: A simply supported prestressed concrete beam spans 12 m and has a rectangular section 400 mm wide by 800 mm deep. The straight tendon has an eccentricity of 250 mm below the centroid and an effective prestress (after all losses) of 1,600 kN. In service the beam carries a superimposed load of 15 kN/m in addition to its self-weight (unit weight of concrete 24 kN/m³). Taking compression as positive, what is the stress at the bottom fiber at midspan?
questions.required: The bottom-fiber stress $f_b$ at midspan under service loads.

solution.title: Stress components
solution.text: Axial, prestress bending and load bending terms:

solution.title: Bottom fiber
solution.text: The load moment produces tension at the bottom, opposing the prestress.

questions.insight: The bottom fiber stays in compression, so the section is uncracked under full service load; the top fiber carries $5.19$ MPa compression.
commonErrors: Leaving out the self-weight moment (8.05 MPa).
Computing the top-fiber stress instead (5.19 MPa).
Adding all three terms regardless of sign (23.94 MPa).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Effective prestress for zero tension at service
questions.stem: A simply supported post-tensioned beam spans 10 m and has a rectangular section 350 mm × 700 mm. At midspan the tendon is 200 mm below the centroid. The beam carries a superimposed service load of 20 kN/m plus its self-weight (concrete unit weight 24 kN/m³). What minimum effective prestress force (after losses) is needed so that the bottom fiber at midspan has **zero** tensile stress under full service load?

solution.title: Load stress at the bottom
solution.text: Tension caused by the service moment:

solution.title: Prestress per unit force
solution.text: Compression at the bottom per newton of prestress (in $10^{-6}$/mm²):

questions.insight: Raising the eccentricity is the most economical way to cut the required force, limited by cover and by the top-fiber tension at transfer.
commonErrors: Leaving out the beam's self-weight (789.5 kN).
Ignoring the axial $P/A$ compression, i.e. $P = M/e$ (1617.5 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Prestress force to balance a uniform load
questions.stem: A simply supported post-tensioned beam spans 14 m. Its parabolic tendon is anchored at the centroid at both ends and has a sag (drape) of 280 mm at midspan. Using the load-balancing concept, what effective prestress force is needed to exactly balance a uniform load of 18 kN/m?
given: Parabolic tendon, sag $e = 0.28\text{ m}$ (anchors at the centroid)

formulas.label: Equivalent upward load of a parabolic tendon

solution.title: Balance with the tendon
solution.text: At midspan the tendon moment $Pe$ equals $M$.

questions.insight: Under the balanced load the beam carries uniform compression $P/A$ with no bending, so it neither sags nor cambers.
commonErrors: Using $wL^2/(4e)$, as if balancing a point load (3150.0 kN).
Using the fixed-end coefficient $wL^2/(12e)$ (1050.0 kN).
Using half the span in $wL^2/(8e)$ (393.75 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Design tensile strength of a bolted plate
questions.stem: A 220 mm × 14 mm steel plate ($F_y = 248$ MPa, $F_u = 400$ MPa) is connected by 20-mm bolts, with two bolt holes in any one cross-section. Use a hole diameter of 23 mm for net-area calculations and take $A_e = A_n$ ($U = 1.0$). Using LRFD with $\phi = 0.90$ for yielding on the gross area and $\phi = 0.75$ for rupture on the net area, what is the design tensile strength of the plate (block shear not considered)?
given: Two holes per section, hole diameter for net area 23 mm

solution.title: Areas
solution.text: Gross area and net area through two holes.

questions.insight: With mild steel's high $F_u/F_y$ ratio, gross yielding often governs plates with few holes; with higher-strength steel or more holes, rupture tends to control.
commonErrors: Taking the net-section rupture value (730.8 kN) without comparing it with yielding.
Omitting $\phi$ on gross yielding (763.8 kN).
Omitting $\phi$ on net-section rupture (974.4 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Design strength of a plate with staggered holes
questions.stem: A 300 mm × 12 mm plate ($F_y = 345$ MPa, $F_u = 450$ MPa) has bolt holes on three gauge lines spaced $g = 75$ mm apart. The holes on the two outer lines are in the same cross-section, and the hole on the middle line is staggered $s = 50$ mm along the plate from them. Use an effective hole diameter of 24 mm, $A_e = A_n$ ($U = 1.0$), $\phi = 0.90$ for gross yielding and $\phi = 0.75$ for net rupture, and the $s^2/4g$ rule for diagonal segments. What is the design tensile strength of the plate (block shear not considered)?
given: Three gauge lines at $g = 75\text{ mm}$; stagger $s = 50\text{ mm}$

formulas.label: Net width along a zigzag path

variables.meaning: Net width along a failure path

solution.title: Straight path
solution.text: Through the two outer holes only:

solution.title: Zigzag path
solution.text: Outer hole → middle hole → other outer hole: three holes and two diagonal segments, each adding $s^2/4g = 8.333$ mm.

questions.insight: Staggering holes lets a zigzag path pick up extra width through the $s^2/4g$ terms; a longer stagger would push the critical path back to the straight line.
commonErrors: Checking only the straight path through two holes (1020.6 kN).
Deducting three holes but omitting the $s^2/4g$ additions (923.4 kN).
Reporting gross yielding (1117.8 kN) even though rupture is smaller.

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Design compressive strength of a wide-flange column
questions.stem: A wide-flange steel column 4.5 m long is pinned at both ends about both axes ($K = 1.0$). Its properties are $A = 9{,}300$ mm², $r_x = 110$ mm and $r_y = 64$ mm, with $F_y = 345$ MPa and $E = 200$ GPa; local buckling does not govern. Use $F_e = \pi^2E/(KL/r)^2$; when $KL/r \le 4.71\sqrt{E/F_y}$, $F_{cr} = 0.658^{F_y/F_e}F_y$; and $\phi_c = 0.90$. What is the design compressive strength $\phi_cP_n$?

solution.title: Governing slenderness
solution.text: Same $KL$ about both axes, so the smaller $r$ governs.

questions.insight: At $KL/r \approx 70$ the column is in the inelastic range, where the critical stress is about 70% of $F_y$; bracing the weak axis at midheight would make the strong axis govern.
commonErrors: Using the strong-axis radius of gyration $r_x$ (2555 kN).
Using the Euler stress $F_e$ as $F_{cr}$, ignoring inelastic behavior (3342 kN).
Reporting the nominal strength $P_n$ without $\phi_c$ (2235 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Allowable live load on a laterally braced steel beam
questions.stem: A simply supported steel floor beam spans 8 m and is continuously braced against lateral-torsional buckling. The section is compact, with plastic section modulus $Z_x = 1.20\times10^6$ mm³ and elastic section modulus $S_x = 1.05\times10^6$ mm³; $F_y = 345$ MPa. The service dead load is 10 kN/m (including self-weight). Using LRFD with $\phi_b = 0.90$, $M_n = F_yZ_x$ and the combination $1.2D + 1.6L$, what is the largest uniform service live load the beam can carry (flexure only)?
given: $L = 8\text{ m}$, continuous lateral support, compact section
questions.required: The maximum uniform service live load $w_L$.

solution.title: Service live load
solution.text: Subtract the factored dead load and divide by 1.6.

questions.insight: A compact, fully braced beam can develop its plastic moment, about 14% more than first yield ($Z_x/S_x = 1.14$); serviceability should still be checked separately.
commonErrors: Using the elastic section modulus $S_x$ (17.97 kN/m).
Omitting $\phi_b$ (24.84 kN/m).
Subtracting the unfactored dead load and ignoring the load factors (36.58 kN/m).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Design shear strength of a bolted lap joint
questions.stem: A lap splice uses four 20-mm diameter high-strength bolts in **single shear**. Take the nominal shear stress of the bolt as $F_{nv} = 372$ MPa and $\phi = 0.75$. Considering bolt shear only, what is the design shear strength of the connection?
questions.required: The design shear strength $\phi R_n$ of the bolt group.
questions.insight: A lap joint loads each bolt on one plane; a butt splice with two cover plates puts each bolt in double shear and doubles the capacity.
commonErrors: Assuming double shear (701.2 kN).
Omitting $\phi$ (467.5 kN).
Computing the strength of one bolt only (87.65 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Design strength of longitudinal fillet welds
questions.stem: A tension angle is connected to a gusset plate by two longitudinal 8-mm fillet welds, each 150 mm long. The electrode has $F_{EXX} = 485$ MPa. Use a weld nominal stress of $0.60F_{EXX}$ on the effective throat ($0.707$ times the leg size) and $\phi = 0.75$; the base metal does not govern. What is the design strength of the welds?
questions.required: The design strength $\phi R_n$ of the welds.

solution.title: Design strength
solution.text: Multiply by the total length and $\phi$.

questions.insight: Fillet welds always fail through the throat in shear, so the leg size must be converted to the throat before computing strength.
commonErrors: Using the leg size as the throat (523.8 kN).
Using $F_{EXX}$ instead of $0.60F_{EXX}$ (617.2 kN).
Omitting $\phi$ (493.8 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Safe uniform load on a timber beam (bending and shear)
questions.stem: A simply supported timber beam has an actual (dressed) section of 150 mm × 300 mm, with the 300-mm side vertical, and spans 3.6 m. The allowable bending stress is $F_b = 10.0$ MPa and the allowable horizontal shear stress is $F_v = 0.80$ MPa. Taking the maximum shear at the support and ignoring deflection and bearing, what is the largest total uniform load (including self-weight) the beam can safely carry?

solution.title: Governing load
solution.text: Shear gives the smaller load and governs.

questions.insight: Short, deep timber beams are often governed by horizontal shear because timber is weak along the grain.
commonErrors: Checking bending only (13.89 kN/m).
Using $V/A$ instead of $1.5V/A$ for the maximum shear stress (20.00 kN/m).
Using $S = bd^2/12$ and checking bending only (6.94 kN/m).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Allowable axial load on a slender timber column
questions.stem: A 150 mm × 200 mm (dressed) timber column has an effective length of 4.0 m about both axes. The allowable compressive stress parallel to grain is $F_c = 11.0$ MPa and $E = 9{,}000$ MPa. Use $d$ = least dimension and $K = 0.671\sqrt{E/F_c}$. The allowable stress is $F'_c = F_c$ for $L_e/d \le 11$; $F'_c = F_c\left[1 - \tfrac{1}{3}\left(\tfrac{L_e/d}{K}\right)^4\right]$ for $11 < L_e/d \le K$; and $F'_c = 0.30E/(L_e/d)^2$ for $K < L_e/d \le 50$. What is the allowable axial load?

variables.meaning: Boundary between intermediate and long columns

solution.title: Allowable load
solution.text: Multiply by the full area, 30 000 mm².

questions.insight: The 0.30 coefficient is roughly the Euler stress divided by a safety factor of about 2.7, so slender timber columns carry only a fraction of their crushing strength.
commonErrors: Using the larger dimension (200 mm) for $L_e/d$ (202.5 kN).
Ignoring slenderness and using $F_cA$ (330.0 kN).
Using the Euler load with no safety factor (312.3 kN).

questions.subject: psad
questions.title: Maximum span of a timber floor joist (bending and deflection)
questions.stem: Timber floor joists with an actual section of 50 mm × 200 mm are spaced at 400 mm on centers and are simply supported. The floor carries a total uniform load (dead plus live) of 4.8 kPa. The allowable bending stress is $F_b = 12$ MPa, $E = 10{,}000$ MPa, and the deflection under total load is limited to span/360. Assuming shear and bearing are adequate, what is the maximum span of the joists?
given: Joist $50 \times 200\text{ mm}$ at 400 mm on centers
questions.required: The maximum span $L$ satisfying both bending and deflection.

variables.meaning: Section modulus and moment of inertia

questions.insight: Deflection, not strength, usually limits the span of floor joists; deeper joists help far more than wider ones because $I$ grows with $d^3$.
commonErrors: Checking bending only (4.08 m).
Using the span/240 limit instead of span/360 (3.82 m).
Using the floor pressure 4.8 kPa as the line load without multiplying by the spacing (2.46 m).
